title: IIT Kharagpur's Solar-Powered Cart Aims to Turn Street Vendors Into Entrepreneurs
excerpt: Unveiled under the institute's Nagar Udyam programme, the three-wheeler vending machine runs on solar power, takes digital payments, segregates waste three ways, and goes home with the vendor at night.
body:
• IIT Kharagpur has unveiled a solar-powered food vending machine mounted on a three-wheeler cart, launched on campus under the programme 'Nagar Udyam - From Street Vendor to Smart Entrepreneur'.
  • The cart combines solar power, digital payment facilities, a bright product display and a three-way waste segregation system, and it can be taken home after business hours instead of permanently occupying public space.
  • Director Suman Chakraborty, who conceived the project, said the goal is to redesign the opportunity around the vendor, not just the cart, as part of the institute's platinum jubilee work.
  • Testing will run through IIT Kharagpur's SETU Cloud Kitchen Connect platform, which is designed to give vendors digital identification, QR-based access, cashless payments, training and cleaner business records.

IIT Kharagpur has built a food vending cart that runs on sunlight, accepts digital payments and goes home with its owner at night. The solar-powered machine, mounted on a three-wheeler, was unveiled on the institute's campus at the inauguration of 'Nagar Udyam - From Street Vendor to Smart Entrepreneur', a programme aimed at giving street vendors the equipment and the digital footing of a small business rather than a pavement pitch, Careers360 reported.

A cart built to move with demand

The design attacks three problems that define street vending in Indian cities: power, place and payments. Solar panels remove the need for a grid connection or a rented shopfront supply. Because the machine sits on a three-wheeler, the vendor can serve different customer groups at different points in the day and take the unit home after business hours, which reduces the need to occupy public space permanently, a recurring source of friction with municipal authorities. A bright product display is built in, along with a three-way waste segregation system, so the cart handles its own refuse sorting rather than leaving it to the street. Digital payment facilities are fitted as standard, putting UPI-style cashless transactions on a cart that would traditionally run on cash alone.

Redesigning the opportunity, not just the cart

The project was conceived by IIT Kharagpur Director Suman Chakraborty and is part of the institute's platinum jubilee plans, framed by the institute as an exercise in translating technology into practical tools for social and economic development. Chakraborty set the ambition plainly at the launch: "Our ambition is not simply to redesign a street cart; it is to redesign the opportunity around the person who runs it. A business that can move with demand, return home at night and connect to clean energy and digital finance can turn an opportunity seeker into a job creator. That is the kind of technology translation IIT Kharagpur stands for."

The digital layer: SETU Cloud Kitchen Connect

The hardware is only half the proposition. For testing, the vending machine will be integrated with the institute's SETU Cloud Kitchen Connect platform, which is intended to provide vendors with digital identification, QR-based access, cashless payment facilities, training and improved business records. Those records matter beyond convenience: a vendor with a documented transaction history is in a stronger position to access credit and formal schemes than one whose entire business runs in cash. The platform has been taking shape on campus this month through the Technology Students' Gymkhana, whose Smart Food Vending Ecosystem launch under SETU Cloud Kitchen Connect set out the same goals of supporting grassroots entrepreneurs, keeping refreshments affordable for students, and promoting responsible food practices, as described in the initiative's campus announcement coverage.

What is still unknown

The launch answers the design questions and leaves the commercial ones open. Neither the institute's announcement nor the launch coverage puts a price on the cart, states how many vendors will receive units in the first phase, or sets a date for deployment beyond the campus testing programme. Those numbers will decide whether Nagar Udyam stays a well-engineered pilot or becomes a template other institutions and municipalities can copy. What is already clear is the model's logic: give the vendor mobility, clean power, a digital identity and a payment trail, and the same person the city treats as an encroachment problem starts to look like a micro-entrepreneur with a balance sheet.
